1.1:
Pharaoh raised himself high in the land and split its people into groups. He oppressed one group: the verse says he slaughtered their sons and let their women live. The game says only that their baby boys were to be taken away.

Verses 28:5–6 give Allah's plan: to favour the oppressed, make them leaders and heirs, and show Pharaoh, Haman and their armies the very thing they feared.
1.2: Ask your child: what does it feel like when someone is unfair to you? What do you wish someone would do?
1.3:
Ask: when bad things happen, does Allah see? This whole story is about Allah helping people who were being hurt.

Ibn Kathir explains that Pharaoh killed the newborn boys of the Children of Israel because he feared a boy would be born among them who would bring about his downfall; the precaution could not stop what Allah had decreed.
1.4:
Talk about plans: what plans does our family make? Allah's plan in this story takes many years, and it starts with a baby.

Where did Pharaoh's fear come from? Ibn Kathir (in his Arabic commentary on 28:4) says the Egyptians had heard it from the Children of Israel: a saying of Ibrahim, after a tyrant of Egypt tried to take his wife Sara, that among his descendants would be one who would bring down the king of Egypt. (Our translation.)
1.5: Name each card as you match it: the river Nile, palm trees, the pyramids... Ask: what would you like to see in Egypt?
2.1:
Musa's mother is inspired to nurse him and, when she fears for him, to put him into the chest and the chest into the river, with the promise that he will be returned to her and made a messenger. 20:39 adds that Allah cast His love over Musa and that he was reared under Allah's watchful eye.

The chest is in the verse (20:39). The commentary adds details the verses do not give: that her house was on the bank of the Nile and that she made a box into a cradle for him. The game's 'getting the chest ready' activity is built on that.
2.2:
Ask: what do you think Musa's mother felt when she heard this message? Being brave doesn't mean not being afraid.

In Majlisi's Hayat al-Qulub, Musa's mother is called Yukabid, which Majlisi says is the most common opinion. The Qur'an does not name her.
2.3: Ask: what would you put in a cradle to keep a baby warm and safe?
2.4:
Ask: what is the bravest thing your mother or father has done for you? This is a good moment to tell your child a story from when they were a baby.

Ibn Kathir passes on what 'they mention' (dhakaru), commentary rather than Qur'an: that Pharaoh's people, afraid of losing their workers, had the boys killed one year and spared the next; Harun was born in a year of sparing and Musa in a year of killing. Musa's mother lived by the Nile; she would hide him in the chest on the water, tied with a rope, whenever someone she feared came in, and one day she forgot to tie it, and the river carried him to Pharaoh's house. (Our translation from the Arabic.)
2.5: Move slowly and gently as you play. Ask: how would you carry something very precious?
2.6: Ask: who watches over you when you sleep? Allah watches over everyone, all the time.
2.7: Look at a river or stream together if you can, or a bowl of water. Ask: where does a river go?
2.8: Ask: what can we do when we are afraid for someone we love? (Make dua, trust Allah, do what we can.)
3.1:
Pharaoh's household picked the child up, not knowing he would become their opponent. Pharaoh's wife said he would be a joy to the eye for her and for Pharaoh, and said: do not kill him; he may be useful to us, or we may adopt him. The game says 'do not harm him'.

The verses do not name her. The commentary names her Asiyah bint Muzahim, says the servant women brought the chest to her unopened, and that Allah filled her heart with love when she saw the child. It also reports Pharaoh's reply, 'For you he may be, but not for me', which the game leaves out.

On 20:39, 'I cast My love over you', the commentary comments that no one saw Musa without loving him. The hearts activity is built on that.
3.2: Ask: who do you think will find the chest? Let your child guess before the next page.
3.3: Asiya is one of the great women of Islam. Ask: why do you think she was kind, even though she lived in Pharaoh's palace?
3.4: Ask: what is the best surprise you have ever found?
3.5: Ask: how do you feel when you see a baby? Allah put love for baby Musa in people's hearts.
3.6: Ask: who loves you? Count them on your fingers together.
3.7: Ask: what does it mean to speak up for someone? Asiya spoke up for a baby she had just met.
3.8: Ask: isn't it amazing that the safest place for Musa was in the king's own palace? How did Allah do that?
3.9: Talk about kind people who stand up for the weak. Who do you know who does that?
4.1:
The heart of Musa's mother became empty; she would have given him away had Allah not strengthened her heart. She told his sister to follow him, and the sister watched from a distance unnoticed. Allah had made him refuse every wet nurse, and the sister offered a household that would bring him up. He was returned to his mother so that she would be comforted and would know that Allah's promise is true.

From the commentary, not the verses: that 'empty' means she could think of nothing but Musa (reported from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrimah, Sa'id bin Jubayr and others); that the sister was the older child; that the queen paid the mother; and that only about a day and a night passed between the distress and the relief, 'and Allah knows best'.

The commentary reports from Ibn Abbas that the palace people doubted the sister and seized her until she explained herself. The game leaves that out.
4.2: Ask your child about their own brother, sister or cousin: how do you look out for each other?
4.3: Play a quiet-footsteps game at home: who can walk the most silently?
4.4: Ask: what does a baby need more than anything? (Their mother, food, sleep, love.)
4.5: Ask: why do you think baby Musa said no to every nurse? Allah was bringing him home.
4.6: Ask: how did Musa's sister help without telling anyone the secret? Being clever and kind together.
4.7: Ask: how do you think his mother felt when she held him again? A lovely moment to hug your child.
4.8: Ask: what promise did Allah make to Musa's mother, and did He keep it?
4.9: Ask your child to tell this chapter to someone else in the family.
4.10: Let your child say each step out loud before tapping.
5.1:
When Musa reached full maturity Allah gave him wisdom and knowledge: 'this is how We reward those who do good'.

The hot coal is not in the Qur'an. The commentary, explaining the prayer 'untie the knot in my tongue' (20:27), says Musa had a lisp from an incident in which he was offered a date and a hot coal and put the coal on his tongue. The tafsir gives it in one sentence and refers elsewhere for the full story; the game adds nothing to it. The commentary says that as a child Musa stayed in Pharaoh's own room.

The sorting activity (safe to eat, or too hot to touch) is a safety game of ours hung on that report.
5.2: Ask: how do you know if something is too hot? Talk about safety at home: the stove, hot tea, matches.
5.3: Make it a real safety lesson: walk around the kitchen together and name what is hot or sharp.
5.4: Ask: what do you want to learn when you grow up? Wisdom is knowing what to do with what you know.
5.5: While solving, ask: what do you think Musa learned in the palace?
5.6: Ask: who gives us wisdom and knowledge? A short dua from the Qur'an children can learn: rabbi zidni 'ilma, 'Lord, increase me in knowledge!' (20:114).
6.1:
Musa entered the city unnoticed and found two men fighting, one of his own people and one an enemy. His kinsman called for help; Musa struck the other with his fist and killed him. The game says the man 'fell down and did not get up again'. Musa said 'this is Satan's work', asked forgiveness and was forgiven, and promised never to support wrongdoers.

Left out: verses 28:18–19, where the same kinsman calls for help again the next day, Musa calls him a troublemaker, and the man lets slip what happened the day before.

In verse 28:20 the man who came running says the authorities are talking about killing Musa. The game says they are 'coming to punish' him.

In a Shia narration (Imam al-Rida) Musa struck the man to stop him from wronging another and did not mean to kill him; 'Satan's work' is read as the fight that Satan stirred up.
6.2:
Ask: what can happen when we act too fast when we are angry? What could Musa have done instead?

In Hayat al-Qulub, Imam al-Rida explains that Musa struck to stop a man who was 'openly leading astray' and did not mean to kill him. In the game Musa calls it the work of Shaytan and asks forgiveness, as the Qur'an tells it.
6.3: Ask: what does a real sorry sound like? Practise one together.
6.4: Hold the hands together with your child. Ask: is there anyone you want to say sorry to?
6.5: Musa did not hide his mistake; he turned to Allah at once. Ask: what do you do when you've done something wrong?
6.6: Ask: who was the man who came running? Someone who cared enough to warn Musa. Who would you warn if they were in danger?
6.7: Ask: what can we say to Allah when we feel afraid? Let your child make up a short dua.
6.8: Ask: how do you think Musa felt leaving his home? Talk about times your family moved or travelled.
7.1:
Musa turned towards Madyan hoping his Lord would guide him. At its water he found men watering flocks and two women holding theirs back; they could not water until the shepherds left, and their father was very old. He watered for them, withdrew to the shade and prayed: 'My Lord, I am in dire need of whatever good You send me.'

The heavy rock is not in the verses. The commentary, on 'the strong, the trustworthy' in 28:26, reports from Umar, Ibn Abbas, Shurayh, Abu Malik, Qatadah, Ibn Ishaq and others that the daughter said Musa had lifted a rock that only ten men could lift. The commentary says he sat beneath a tree (Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, As-Suddi).

The tafsir also mentions, with 'and Allah knows best', a report that an angel on a horse showed Musa the way. The game does not use it.
7.2: Ask: how long can you walk? Count your steps on your next walk together.
7.3: Ask: what did Musa notice that others didn't? (Two young women waiting.) Noticing people who need help is the first step to helping.
7.4: Ask: what would you do if you saw someone left out, waiting at the back?
7.5: Ask: is it better to be strong, or to use your strength to help? Musa used his for others.
7.6: Try lifting something heavy together, then something light. Ask: what is heavy for you that is easy for a grown-up?
7.7: Ask: how many animals have you helped look after? Count the sheep together as you play.
7.8: Musa had nothing left, so he asked Allah. Ask: what do you ask Allah for when you need something?
7.9: Musa's prayer under the tree can be learnt: rabbi inni lima anzalta ilayya min khayrin faqir, 'My Lord, I am in dire need of whatever good thing You may send me' (28:24).
7.10: Name each card from the well as you match it.
8.1:
One of the two women came walking shyly with her father's invitation. Musa told his story and the old man said: do not be afraid, you are safe now. A daughter said: hire him, the best to hire is the strong and trustworthy. The father offered marriage to one of his daughters for eight years of work, ten if Musa chose, and Musa agreed. The verses do not name the father.

From the commentary, not the verses: Musa asked her to walk behind him and throw a pebble to show the way (reported from Umar, Ibn Abbas and others, as her explanation of 'trustworthy'); and Musa completed the longer term, ten years, which the tafsir quotes from al-Bukhari on the authority of Ibn Abbas.

Shia narrations name the old man as the Prophet Shu'ayb; Sunni scholars are divided on it, and the verses do not say. The same narrations also tell the two details above.
8.2: Ask: how did Musa show respect? Talk about good manners when walking with others.
8.3: Ask: how do you give directions to someone? Practise: 'left, right, straight on.'
8.4: In the Shia narrations (Hayat al-Qulub) the old man of Madyan is the Prophet Shu'ayb; Sunni scholars are divided. Ask: what does it feel like when someone says 'you are safe now'?
8.5: 'The best person to hire is one who is strong and trustworthy' (28:26). Ask: what makes you a good helper at home?
8.6: Ask: which is more important, being strong or being honest? Can someone be both?
8.7: Ask: what do people promise when they marry? Talk about a wedding your family remembers.
8.8: Count the ten years together. Ask: what will you be doing in ten years?
8.9: Ask: why do sheep need a shepherd? Many prophets were shepherds for a time.
8.10: While solving, ask your child to describe life in Madyan.
9.1:
When his term was complete Musa was travelling with his family and saw a fire. He told them to wait: he might bring a burning brand, or find guidance there. He was called: 'Musa! I am your Lord. Take off your shoes: you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa. I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed. I am Allah; there is no god but Me. So worship Me and keep up the prayer so that you remember Me.' Verse 28:30 says the call came from the right side of the valley, from a tree on blessed ground.

The pictures show a fire and a light, and nothing else. Allah is not shown, and no angel is shown anywhere in this game.
9.2: Ask: what would you do if you saw a fire in the dark? Talk about fire safety too.
9.3: Turn off the lights for a moment and look for a small light together. Ask: how does the light help?
9.4: Ask: what do you think Musa expected to find at the fire?
9.5: Ask: why do we take off our shoes at the mosque? Respect for holy places.
9.6: A good moment to remind your child: shoes off at the door of the mosque, and placed neatly.
9.7: 'Keep up the prayer to remember Me' (20:14). Ask: why do we pray? To remember Allah.
9.8: Ask your child to be still and quiet for a minute, and listen. What can you hear?
9.9: Talk about it: Musa is called kalimullah, the one Allah spoke to.
10.1:
Asked what was in his right hand, Musa said it was his staff: he leaned on it, kept his sheep in order with it, and had other uses for it. Thrown down, it became a fast-moving snake and he turned to flee; he was told to pick it up without fear and it would return to its former state. His hand, drawn out from his side, came out white and unharmed. These were two signs for Pharaoh and his chiefs.

'Shone like the moon' is from the commentary: the hand came out 'shining as if it were a half moon', free of any disease (reported from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrimah, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak and As-Suddi); Al-Hasan al-Basri said 'as if it were a lamp'.
10.2: Ask: what do you think will happen to the staff? Let your child guess.
10.3: Ask: who made the staff become a snake? Only Allah can do that. Musa did not do it by himself.
10.4: Ask: how did Musa feel when his hand shone? Surprised? Happy?
10.5: Ask: what are some of the signs of Allah we can see every day? (The sun rising, rain, a baby growing.)
10.6: Ask: is it easy to go and speak to someone who is unkind? What would help you be brave?
10.7: Let your child explain each match out loud.
10.8: Name each card from that night as you match it.
11.1:
How Musa met Harun again is not described in the verses; 20:42 says 'go, you and your brother', so the game says only that Harun went with him.

Musa asked: lift up my heart, ease my task, untie my tongue so they may understand my words, and give me a helper from my family, Harun my brother; strengthen me through him and let him share my task, so that we may glorify and remember You much. He was told: your request is granted.

Verses 28:33–35: Musa says he killed one of their men and fears they may kill him, and that Harun is the better speaker. The game says only that he was afraid of what they might do to him. Verses 20:42–46: go, both of you; speak to him gently so that he may take heed or show respect; do not be afraid, I am with you both, hearing and seeing.

The commentary reports from Ibn Abbas that Harun was made a prophet at that same moment, and that A'ishah agreed with a man who said no brother was ever more useful to his brother than Musa was in this prayer.
11.2: Musa's prayer is a beautiful one to learn: rabbishrah li sadri, wa yassir li amri (20:25-26). Many families say it before exams or a new school year.
11.3: Ask: who helps you be brave? Musa asked for his brother. Who would you ask for?
11.4: Say the prayer together line by line before tapping.
11.5: Ask: did Allah listen to Musa? Does Allah listen to you? Yes, always.
11.6: Ask: what is it like to do something hard with a brother, sister or friend beside you?
11.7: Allah told them to speak gently, even to Pharaoh. Ask: is it easy to be gentle with someone who is unkind? Why is it better?
11.8: Practise saying the same sentence gently and harshly. Ask: which one would you listen to?
11.9: Ask: what gentle words do you use at home? Make a list together.
12.1:
The two brothers say: we are messengers of your Lord; send the Children of Israel with us and do not oppress them. When Musa brought clear signs, Pharaoh's people called them conjuring tricks never heard of from their forefathers. Pharaoh accused Musa of coming to drive them from their land with sorcery and demanded an appointment; Musa named the day of the feast, with the people gathered when the sun is high.

The long exchange about who the Lord is (20:49–55) is left out of the game.
12.2: Ask: what signs did Allah give Musa? Can your child remember both?
12.3: Ask: why do you think Pharaoh did not believe, even after seeing the signs?
12.4: Ask: what does it mean to be stubborn? Have you ever not wanted to listen, even when someone was right?
12.5: Ask: how do you think Musa felt when Pharaoh mocked him?
12.6: Ask: why did Musa choose a day when everyone was there, in daylight? So everyone could see the truth.
12.7: Ask: what festivals do we celebrate? What do people do on Eid?
12.8: Count the people as they come. Ask: why would everyone come to watch?
12.9: While solving, ask: what is happening in this picture?
13.1: Pharaoh gathered his resources and returned. Musa warned the sorcerers not to invent lies against Allah. They asked whether he would throw first; he told them to throw. Through their sorcery their ropes and staffs seemed to him to be moving, and Musa was inwardly alarmed. He was told: do not be afraid, you have the upper hand; throw what is in your right hand and it will swallow what they have produced, which is only a sorcerer's trick. The sorcerers threw themselves down and said: we believe in the Lord of Harun and Musa.
13.2: Musa warned the magicians not to make up lies about Allah. Ask: is a trick the same as a lie?
13.3: Ask: why do you think Musa let them go first?
13.4: Ask: have you ever seen a magic trick? Did it really change anything, or only look like it?
13.5: Ask: how can we tell what is real and what is a trick? Looking closely helps.
13.6: Even prophets feel afraid. Ask: what did Allah tell Musa? Whenever you are afraid, you can remember that Allah is with you.
13.7: Ask: what do you think will happen when Musa throws the staff?
13.8: Ask: who was stronger, the magic or the sign of Allah?
13.9: Ask: how did the magicians feel when they saw this? Surprised? Amazed?
13.10: The magicians changed their minds in a moment. Ask: is it brave to say 'I was wrong'?
13.11: Ask: what made the magicians believe? They knew tricks, so they knew this was real.
14.1:
Pharaoh said: how dare you believe before I give you permission? He threatened to cut off their hands and feet on opposite sides and crucify them on palm trunks. The game says only that he would punish them terribly. They answered that they would never prefer him to the clear signs and to their Creator: 'decide whatever you will: you can only decide matters of this present life.'

Verse 40:28: a believing man of Pharaoh's family who had hidden his faith said, 'How can you kill a man just for saying, My Lord is Allah?' The game says 'hurt'. Verse 66:11 gives the prayer of Pharaoh's wife. The Qur'an does not say at what point in the story the believing man spoke or the queen prayed; the game places them here.

Verses 28:38–39: Pharaoh tells his chiefs he knows of no god for them but himself, and orders Haman to bake clay bricks and build a tall building so that he may climb to Musa's God. The verses fetched for this game do not say what became of the building, so neither does the game.

Shia narrations name the believer of Pharaoh's family Hizqil.
14.2: Ask: what does it mean to choose the truth, even when it is hard?
14.3: Talk about courage: who is the bravest person you know?
14.4:
Ask: is it brave to speak up in a crowd? The believer in Pharaoh's family did it (40:28).

In Hayat al-Qulub, the believer in Pharaoh's family is named Hizqil. The Qur'an does not name him.
14.5: Asiya's prayer: 'My Lord, build me a house near You in the Garden' (66:11). Ask: what would you ask Allah for?
14.6: Hold the hands together and say Asiya's prayer slowly.
14.7: Ask: can people build their way to Allah? What did Pharaoh misunderstand?
14.8: Build a tower of cups or blocks together. Ask: how high can it go before it falls?
14.9: Ask your child which brave person in this chapter they liked best, and why.
15.1:
Pharaoh's people were afflicted with years of drought and crop failure; when good came they claimed it as their due, and when harm came they blamed Musa. They said they would never believe whatever sign he brought. Then came the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood, 'all clear signs'. Each time they asked Musa to pray and promised to believe and release the Children of Israel, and each time they broke the promise.

Details from the commentary, not the verses. The 'flood': Ibn Abbas said it was heavy rain that ruined crops and fruit; he is also reported to have said mass death, and Mujahid said water carrying plague, so the early scholars differed. The locusts eating the nails of the doors is reported from Mujahid. The third sign (qummal): Ibn Abbas said grain weevils, or small wingless locusts; Al-Hasan and Sa'id bin Jubayr said small black insects; the game says 'tiny bugs in the grain'. Frogs in the houses, food, pots and clothes is from Sa'id bin Jubayr and Ibn Ishaq.

The fifth sign is blood: the tafsir says rivers, wells and containers of water turned to blood. The game says the water 'turned red'.
15.2: Ask: what does rain do for crops? When can too much rain be a problem?
15.3: Ask: have you ever seen locusts or grasshoppers? What do they eat?
15.4: Ask: how do farmers protect their crops today?
15.5: Ask: which would you find worst, the bugs or the frogs? Make it light-hearted.
15.6: Ask your child to count the frogs out loud as they find them.
15.7: Ask: why did Allah send these signs? To give Pharaoh's people a chance to change.
15.8: Ask: is a promise made when you're in trouble still a promise when the trouble goes away?
15.9: Ask: who did they ask for help? Musa prayed, and Allah lifted the trouble.
15.10: Ask: have you ever made a promise and forgotten it? How can we keep promises better?
15.11: Ask: what should they have done? (Keep their promise, believe.)
15.12: Let your child name the five signs in order before tapping.
16.1:
Verse 20:77: 'Go out at night with My servants and strike a dry path for them across the sea. Have no fear of being overtaken.' Verses 26:60–62: Pharaoh and his people pursued them at sunrise; when the two sides came in sight of each other Musa's followers said, 'We shall definitely be caught', and Musa said, 'No, my Lord is with me: He will guide me.'

The commentary says they were caught up with at the shore, the sea in front and Pharaoh behind. The lamps in the 'wake the families' activity are ours.
16.2: Ask: why did they have to be so quiet? Play a quiet game at home.
16.3: Ask: if you had to leave at night, what would you take?
16.4: Ask: how do you think the people felt following Musa in the dark? Trust is following someone you know is good.
16.5: Ask: why do you think Pharaoh chased them? He did not want to let them go.
16.6: Ask: what would you do with the sea in front and an army behind? Musa's answer is on the next page.
16.7: 'No! My Lord is with me. He will guide me' (26:62). A sentence worth learning by heart for scary moments.
16.8: Ask: when you are afraid, what can you say? Practise Musa's words together.
16.9: While solving, ask: what do you think will happen next?
17.1:
Verses 26:63–66: 'Strike the sea with your staff.' It parted, each side like a mighty mountain; Musa and all his companions were saved and the others were drowned. The game says the sea 'came crashing back' and that the army 'was gone'. Verses 10:90–92: as he was drowning Pharaoh said he believed in the God of the Children of Israel, and was answered, 'Now? When you had always been a rebel?' Only his body was saved, as a sign for those after him.

From the commentary, not the verses: the twelve paths, one for each tribe (reported from Ibn Abbas); the openings like windows in the water through which they saw one another (As-Suddi); and the wind sent to dry the sea bed. The commentary gives an account in which the angels Jibril and Mika'il ride at the sea; the game does not use it.

Ashura: the tafsir quotes al-Bukhari, from Ibn Abbas, that the Prophet ﷺ found the Jews of Madinah fasting the day Musa was given victory over Pharaoh and said, 'You have more right to Musa than they, so fast it.' The Prophet ﷺ is mentioned in the narration and is not shown.
17.2: Ask: who made the sea open, Musa or Allah? Musa struck; Allah opened it.
17.3: Ask your child to imagine walking between two walls of water. What would you see? Fish?
17.4: It is told (in the commentary) that there were twelve paths, one for each family. Ask: why would each family have its own path?
17.5: Ask: what does the wind do? Can you feel it today?
17.6: Count the twelve paths together, slowly.
17.7: Ask: how do you think the people felt walking across? Scared? Amazed? Thankful?
17.8: Say al-hamdu lillah together. Ask: what are you thankful for today?
17.9: This page can be sad. Explain gently: Pharaoh chose not to listen, again and again, until it was too late.
17.10: Ask: why is it important to believe and do good now, not only when we are in trouble?
17.11: Allah kept Pharaoh's body 'as a sign' (10:92). Ask: what lesson does Pharaoh's story teach?
17.12: Many Muslims fast on 'Ashura, and the day before or after it. Ask your family about your own traditions for 'Ashura.
17.13: Ask your child: who saves us when we are in trouble? Make a short dua of thanks together.
17.14: Let your child tell the whole crossing in their own words.
18.1:
Verse 2:57: clouds were made to shade them, and manna and quails were sent down: 'Eat the good things We have provided for you.' Verse 2:60: Musa prayed for water for his people and was told to strike the rock with his staff; twelve springs gushed out and each group knew its drinking place.

The commentary reports from Ibn Abbas that it was a square stone and that three springs came from each side, one spring for each tribe. The game does not say what manna looked like; the sparkles in the gathering activity are only a stand-in.
18.2: Ask: what is your favourite food? Who gives it to us in the end?
18.3: Ask: what would it be like to find breakfast on the ground every morning?
18.4: Count the birds together. Ask: have you seen quails or other small birds near your home?
18.5: Ask: how does it feel to be very thirsty? Have a glass of water together and say bismillah.
18.6: Count the springs out loud, all twelve.
18.7: Ask: why do you think each family got its own spring? Sharing fairly keeps the peace.
18.8: Ask: how many springs, and how many families? Twelve and twelve.
18.9: Name each gift of the desert as you match it.
19.1:
Allah appointed thirty nights for Musa and added ten, making forty. Musa told Harun to take his place and act rightly. On the mountain Musa asked to see his Lord and was told: 'You will never see Me, but look at that mountain: if it remains firmly in its place, you will see Me.' When his Lord revealed Himself to the mountain He made it crumble, and Musa fell unconscious. On recovering he said: 'Glory be to You! To You I turn in repentance! I am the first to believe!' He was told to hold on to what he had been given and be thankful, and was given the Tablets.

The picture shows a mountain crumbling and nothing else. Allah is never shown.
19.2: Count to thirty, then add ten. Ask: what could you do every day for forty days?
19.3: Ask: have you ever climbed a big hill or a mountain? How did it feel at the top?
19.4: Ask: what is something you wish you could see? Some things are too great for our eyes.
19.5: Ask: if a mountain could not stand it, how great must Allah be?
19.6: Ask your child to describe the mountain in their own words.
19.7: Musa said: 'Glory be to You! To You I turn in repentance! I am the first to believe!' (7:143). Ask: what does subhanallah mean? (Glory be to Allah.) Say it together.
19.8: Ask: what did Allah give Musa? (The Tablets, His words.) What has Allah given us? (The Qur'an.)
19.9: While solving, ask your child what Musa is holding.
19.10: Ask: what are three things you are thankful for today?
20.1:
In Musa's absence the Samiri led the people astray. They had thrown the jewellery they carried into the fire and he brought out a calf that made a lowing sound; it gave them no answer and had no power to harm or benefit them. Harun told them it was a test and that their Lord is the Lord of Mercy; they refused to stop until Musa returned. Musa came back angry and grieved, threw down the Tablets and seized his brother by the hair and beard; Harun said the people had overpowered him and almost killed him. Musa prayed for forgiveness for himself and his brother, told the Samiri to go away, and said the calf would be ground down and scattered in the sea. The people later regretted what they had done (7:149).

The game says Musa 'put down' the Tablets and 'took hold of' his brother, and that the people 'would not listen' to Harun.

From the commentary: Mujahid said the calf's sound came from the wind blowing through it; Ibn Abbas, by way of Ibn Ishaq, said the Samiri came from a people who worshipped cows. What the Samiri says he 'saw' and took a handful of (20:96) is explained in the commentary as the track of the angel Jibril's horse; the game leaves it out.
20.2: Ask: can something look special and still be useless? Talk about things that glitter.
20.3: Ask: what can Allah do that nothing else can? (Hear us, help us, guide us.)
20.4: Ask: why do you think the people made the calf? They were impatient and forgot.
20.5: Ask your child to explain why only Allah deserves worship.
20.6: Ask: how did Harun try to help? Sometimes speaking up is hard, but right.
20.7: Ask: is it all right to feel angry? What should we do with that feeling?
20.8: Ask: why was the calf ground to dust? So no one could worship it again.
20.9: Ask: what are things that can distract us from Allah today? (Screens, toys, wanting more.)
20.10: Ask: what can we do when we've made a mistake as a group, as a family or a class?
20.11: Let your child say each step out loud before tapping.
21.1:
Musa told his people that Allah commands them to sacrifice a cow. They asked if he was mocking them, then asked what sort (neither old nor young, but in between), what colour (bright yellow, pleasing to the eye), and exactly which (unblemished, not trained to plough the earth or water the fields). They slaughtered it, 'though they almost failed to do so'.

Left for parents: verses 2:72–73 give the reason. A person had been killed and the people were accusing one another; they were told to strike the body with part of the cow, and so Allah showed them how He gives life to the dead. The game tells the cow and the questions, and says only that Allah used it to bring out a truth some of them had been hiding, which is the wording of 2:72.

The cow's owner who was kind to his father is from a Shia narration (Imam al-Rida), where Musa says that kindness to parents raises a person high.
21.2: Ask: is it better to do what you're asked straight away, or to ask lots of questions to avoid doing it?
21.3: Ask: what colour cow would you choose? Have some fun with it.
21.4: Ask: what happens when people make simple things complicated?
21.5: In Majlisi's Hayat al-Qulub, Imam al-Rida tells that the cow belonged to a boy who would not wake his sleeping father, even to make a sale, and was rewarded for it; kindness to parents raises a person high. Ask: how can you be kind to your parents today?
21.6: Ask your child to describe the cow before tapping it: yellow, no marks.
21.7: Ask: why is it better to listen the first time?
21.8: Ask: what is one thing you could do this week the first time you're asked?
21.9: Let your child say the three questions in order before tapping.
22.1:
Musa reminded his people of Allah's blessings and told them to enter the holy land Allah had ordained for them and not turn back. They said a fearsome people lived there and they would not enter until those people left. Two men whom Allah had blessed said: go in through the gate, and you will be victorious; put your trust in Allah. The people answered: 'You and your Lord go and fight; we will stay here.' Musa said he had authority over no one but himself and his brother. The land was forbidden to them for forty years, during which they would wander.

The verses do not name the two men.
22.2:
Ask: what are you afraid of trying? Being afraid is normal; what matters is what we do next.

You may meet stories of giants in that land, above all 'Uj bin 'Anaq, said to be more than three thousand cubits tall and to have outlived the Flood. Ibn Kathir rejects them firmly: they are 'reports made up by the Children of Israel', 'something one is ashamed to mention', against the authentic hadith that Adam was sixty cubits tall and people have grown smaller since; the claim that he survived the Flood is 'a lie and a fabrication', since the Qur'an says the unbelievers were drowned; and 'whether a man called 'Uj bin 'Anaq existed at all is doubtful, and Allah knows best'.

The story that a giant scooped up Musa's twelve scouts in his sleeve with his fruit: Ibn Kathir says of its chain, 'there is doubt about it'. (Our translations from the Arabic.)
22.3:
Ask: what did the two brave men trust? Allah's promise.

Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, As-Suddi and others name the two brave men: Yusha' bin Nun (Joshua) and Kalib (Caleb) (in Ibn Kathir).
22.4: Ask your child to say the brave men's words in their own way.
22.5: Ask: is saying 'you go, I'll stay here' fair? What would you have said?
22.6: Ask: how do you think Musa felt when his people would not listen?
22.7:
Ask: what does it feel like to go round in circles? Sometimes we must wait for a long time.

You may hear what came after the forty years. Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn Abbas that Musa and Harun died during the wandering, and that Yusha' bin Nun then led the next generation into Jerusalem; as the sun was about to set on a Friday, Yusha' asked Allah to hold it back until the city was won. Ibn Kathir says there is evidence for this in the Sahih.
22.8: Ask your child to think of one brave thing they could do this week.
23.1:
Musa told his servant he would not stop until he reached the place where the two seas meet. There they forgot their fish, which made its way into the sea. Later, tired and asking for the meal, the servant remembered: he had forgotten the fish by the rock, and only Satan made him forget. Musa said that was the place they were seeking, and they retraced their steps. They found a servant of Allah who had been given mercy and knowledge. He warned Musa he would not be able to bear with him patiently; Musa promised patience; the condition was that Musa ask about nothing until he himself spoke of it.

From a hadith of Ubayy bin Ka'b in al-Bukhari, as quoted in the commentary, not from the verses: Musa was asked who was the most learned of people and said 'I am', and was told of a servant who knew more; he was told to carry a fish in a basket and that he would find the man where he lost the fish; the servant boy was Yusha bin Nun; the water stood like an arch over the fish's path; and the man's name was al-Khidr.

Al-Khidr means 'the green one': wherever he sat, the bare ground turned green. Al-Bukhari reports this from the Prophet ﷺ, and the Shia narrations have it from the Imams.
23.2:
Musa wanted to keep learning, even though he was a great prophet. Ask: what would you travel far to learn?

Why did Musa set out? In a hadith in al-Bukhari (quoted by Ibn Kathir), Musa was asked who was the most learned person, and he said: I am. Allah rebuked him 'because he did not refer the knowledge to Allah', and told him of a servant at the meeting of the two seas who knew what Musa did not.

Musa said he would travel 'for a long time' (huqub): Ibn Kathir reports that 'Abdullah bin 'Amr said eighty years, Mujahid seventy, and Ibn Abbas a lifetime.
23.3: Look at a map together for a place where two seas or rivers meet. Ask: what would it look like?
23.4:
Ask: what would you think if you saw a fish jump into the sea?

One narration in al-Bukhari (quoted by Ibn Kathir) says there was a spring at the foot of the rock called al-Hayat, the Spring of Life, whose water brought to life whatever it touched; a drop touched the fish, and it slipped into the sea.
23.5: Ask your child to follow the fish with their finger as it swims.
23.6:
Ask: have you ever forgotten to tell someone something important? Yusha forgot too.

You may meet a report (in Ibn Jarir al-Tabari) that Musa's young helper drank from the Spring of Life, became immortal, and was set adrift in a boat until the Day of Judgement. Ibn Kathir: 'a weak chain; al-Hasan [bin 'Umara] is abandoned as a narrator, and his father is unknown'. The authentic hadiths name the helper as Yusha' bin Nun, who led the people after Musa.
23.7: Ask: what do we do when we realise we went the wrong way? Turn back.
23.8: Count the footsteps back to the rock together.
23.9: Ask: who is a teacher who knows things you don't know?
23.10:
Ask: what makes things grow green? Al-Khidr's name means 'the green one'.

You may hear that al-Khidr is still alive. Ibn Kathir reports that al-Nawawi and Ibn al-Salah leaned that way, but says 'none of that is authentic; the best known are the hadiths of condolence, and their chain is weak'. Other scholars held that he died, citing 21:34 ('We have not granted everlasting life to any other human being before you'), and that he never came to the Prophet ﷺ, though he would have followed him had he been alive. (Our translation.)

The meaning of his name is authentic: al-Bukhari reports the Prophet ﷺ saying he was called al-Khidr because he sat on a patch of dry, withered plants, and it stirred green behind him.
23.11: Musa asked politely to learn. Ask: how do we ask a teacher for help?
23.12: Ask: is it easy to wait without asking questions? What is the hardest thing to be patient about?
23.13: Ask your child what Musa promised, and whether they think he can keep it.
24.1:
In the boat the man made a hole in it, and Musa objected. Verse 18:74 then says they met a young boy and the man killed him, and Musa protested more strongly. The game does not tell this to small children: it says only that the second thing was about a boy and is 'a story for when you are older'. The explanation in 18:80–81 is that the boy's parents were people of faith, that he would have burdened them with wickedness and disbelief, and that their Lord would give them a better child in his place.

The third: a town refused them food, and the man repaired a wall that was about to fall; Musa said he could have taken payment. The explanations: the boat belonged to needy people who worked at sea, and a king was seizing every sound boat by force; the wall belonged to two orphans, with a treasure beneath it, and their father had been righteous. 'I did not do these things of my own accord.'

From the hadith in al-Bukhari quoted in the commentary, not the verses: the crew knew al-Khidr and carried them without a fare; the bird that dipped its beak in the sea and what al-Khidr said about knowledge; and the Prophet's ﷺ words, 'We wish that Musa had been patient, so that Allah would have told us more about the two of them.' The closing sentence about good hidden inside a thing that looks bad is the game's own summary of the lesson.
24.2:
Ask: what would you think if someone made a hole in a boat? Would you ask why?

In the hadith in al-Bukhari, the boat's crew recognised al-Khidr and carried them for free, which is why Musa was so shocked when al-Khidr damaged it.
24.3: Ask: how much water can a bird take in its beak, compared to the whole sea? That is how little we know, next to Allah.
24.4: Talk about it: all the books in the world are like a bird's sip from the sea. How does that make you feel about Allah?
24.5: If your child is older and asks, this is in Surah al-Kahf (18:74, 18:80-81); otherwise it is enough to say it was hard for Musa to understand.
24.6: Ask: why would al-Khidr mend the wall for people who would not feed them? Doing good without being thanked.
24.7: Ask: what can you fix or help with at home, even if nobody says thank you?
24.8: Ask: have you ever had to say goodbye to a teacher or friend? What did they teach you?
24.9: Ask: can something that looks bad turn out to protect us? Think of an example together.
24.10: Ask: who looks after orphans? The verse says their father was a righteous man (18:82).
24.11: Ask: what treasure would you hide for your children one day?
24.12: Let your child explain each secret in their own words.
24.13: In Hayat al-Qulub, Imam al-Sadiq gives al-Khidr's parting advice to Musa: do not be stubborn, do not laugh without reason, and do not look for the faults of others. Ask: which one is hardest?
24.14: Ask: what could we have learned if Musa had kept quiet? Patience opens doors.
24.15: Ask your child what they learned from al-Khidr.
25.1:
Verse 28:43: Musa was given the Scripture, to give people insight, guidance and mercy, so that they might take heed. The chapter looks back over the whole story.

This game tells a large part of what the Qur'an says about Musa, not all of it: the story is spread over many surahs. A good next step with an older child is to read Surah Ta-Ha (20) and Surah Al-Qasas (28) together.
25.2:
Ask: when is Allah with you? Always, everywhere.

You may meet two hadiths about Musa in al-Bukhari that surprise people. In one, the angel of death came to Musa and Musa struck him; Allah then offered Musa a year of life for every hair his hand would cover on an ox's back (al-Bukhari 1339 and 3407). In the other, Musa bathed alone and a stone ran off with his clothes, and he chased after it (in al-Bukhari's book on the Prophets; check the number on sunnah.com before quoting it). Both are in al-Bukhari; scholars explain them at length, and they are best read with a teacher.
25.3: Ask: what book did Allah give us? The Qur'an is light and guidance for us.
25.4: Let your child tell the whole story of Musa from the river to the sea.
25.5: Ask: who was your favourite person in the story? Asiya? Musa's sister? The magicians?
25.6: Name each card as you match it, and say one thing about that part of the story.
25.7: While solving, ask: what would you like to remember from Musa's story?
